subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Gravitational Waves: A New Messenger
description: A 60-second lesson on Gravitational Waves: A New Messenger.

hook.text: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916. It took exactly 100 years to detect them.

buildup.text: LIGO uses lasers bouncing in 4 km tunnels to detect space stretching by less than a proton's width.

discovery.text: On September 14, 2015, LIGO detected two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds.

twist.text: The detection almost didn't happen. LIGO had just finished a major upgrade and was in its engineering test run.

climax.text: Weiss, Thorne, and Barish won the 2017 Nobel Prize. Gravitational-wave astronomy is now a thriving new field.

punchline.text: A century from prediction to proof. Now we can hear the cosmos.

quiz.question: What event did LIGO detect in its landmark 2015 observation?
options: Two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away
A neutron star colliding with a black hole
The Big Bang's primordial gravitational waves

details.summary: On September 14, 2015, LIGO directly detected gravitational waves for the first time — ripples in spacetime from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away.
details.whyItMatters: Gravitational wave detection is one of the greatest scientific achievements ever. It opened a new 'window' on the universe — allowing us to observe phenomena invisible to light, like black hole and neutron star mergers, and test gravity in extreme…
takeaways: LIGO detected gravitational waves from merging black holes in 2015
This confirmed Einstein's century-old prediction from general relativity
It opened a new way to observe the universe beyond light

faq.question: How does LIGO detect gravitational waves?
faq.answer: LIGO uses two 4-kilometer laser interferometer arms at right angles. A passing gravitational wave stretches one arm and compresses the other by an impossibly tiny amount — about 1/10,000th the width of a proton. Comparing laser beams in both arms detects this change.

faq.question: What can gravitational waves tell us that light cannot?
faq.answer: Gravitational waves pass through matter unimpeded, reaching us from events hidden from light — like the moments of black hole formation, the interiors of supernovae, and the first instants after the Big Bang.
